scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original independent C1 Plastic Ocean review-based test proposal pending human audit.

tabs.title: Aesthetics and Argument
tabs.description: Analyse the documentary's artistic and rhetorical choices.

tabs.title: Critical Judgement
tabs.description: Apply the review's standards to new documentary choices.

questions.q: What distinction is established by the claim that knowing what to feel is not knowing what to do?
choices: A well-made film should avoid any emotional response.
Viewers rarely understand a clear visual metaphor.
Emotional clarity is not equivalent to understanding possible action.
Environmental problems can be solved by stronger feelings alone.
questions.explanation: The opening acknowledges the force of the wrapper image while questioning its practical usefulness.

questions.q: Why is the beauty of the cleaners' work described as 'double-edged'?
choices: It grants visibility to their labour but obscures their conditions and influence.
It gives the cleaners too much time to speak.
It proves that the director has invented the night shift.
It makes waste look less visible in the square.
questions.explanation: The reviewer notes that attractive images can conceal the workers' circumstances.

questions.q: How does the cleaner's remark about the square being empty at its cleanest function?
choices: It suggests that cleaners prefer working in complete silence.
It proves that litter occurs only during the day.
It allows the director to explain exactly how waste contracts operate.
It draws attention to necessary labour that the public seldom witnesses.
questions.explanation: The irony exposes how the finished square is seen while the work remains hidden.

questions.q: What distinguishes the council-desk interview from the documentary's more symbolic scenes?
choices: It claims that reusable cups are too expensive everywhere.
It allows practical constraints to remain complex instead of immediately moralised.
It gives organisers a single perfect answer.
It avoids showing a person with institutional responsibility.
questions.explanation: The facilities manager discusses storage, training and washing costs without a neat solution.

questions.q: What rhetorical effect does repeating the teenager's bottle-dropping scene have?
choices: It explains why the proposed deposit scheme is profitable.
It makes the film's earlier measurements more reliable.
It shifts attention from systems to individual guilt.
It gives the teenager a chance to defend their decision.
questions.explanation: The review says the repeated image replaces an institutional discussion with a personal moral lesson.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer regard the unequal treatment of cleaners, manager and teenager as meaningful?
choices: How people are named or represented influences the argument viewers receive.
All participants must have exactly the same time on screen.
An environmental film should avoid real people.
The camera's position has no impact on interpretation.
questions.explanation: The review highlights the asymmetry between unnamed workers, a speaking manager and a symbolic teenager.

questions.q: What makes the volunteer's admission of extra washing trips credible?
choices: It proves that plastic cups are preferable in every context.
It shows that no one collected any waste at the event.
It allows the director to remove all uncertain conclusions.
It presents an unforeseen cost as something to examine, not a reason to abandon the idea.
questions.explanation: The reviewer praises the admission because it invites revision rather than applause.

questions.q: A filmmaker says, 'Every moving scene must be followed by a spreadsheet.' How would the reviewer respond?
choices: Spreadsheets are the only reliable form of documentary evidence.
Cinema can use emotion and surprise, but should not systematically hide causation.
Any environmental film should become a formal council report.
A moving film is unable to discuss practical systems.
questions.explanation: The sixth paragraph explicitly rejects turning the whole documentary into a council report.

questions.q: What would the reviewer most likely want the film to explore after the facilities manager speaks?
choices: Who bears costs and has the power to implement a deposit scheme.
Whether the manager appears sympathetic enough on camera.
How quickly the teenage littering scene can be repeated.
Which colour should be chosen for the square's bins.
questions.explanation: The review identifies storage, staff training and washing equipment as significant complexities.

questions.q: Which revision would best address the documentary's principal missed opportunity?
choices: Replace all cleaner interviews with scenic images.
Focus more closely on the teenager's personal guilt.
Use visual storytelling to reveal how waste-management systems function.
Remove the admission that some reuse schemes need adjustment.
questions.explanation: The closing paragraph wants the systems around the wrapper to be made as visible as the wrapper itself.
